title: New descendants mainly exterminate their parent species and closest relatives

fields.label: Label
fields.value: New descendants mainly exterminate their parent species and closest relatives

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because competition is most severe between the most similar forms, the improved descendants of a species generally cause the extinction of the parent species and of its nearest allies in the same genus.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence the improved and modified descendants of a species will generally cause the extermination of the parent-species; and if many new forms have been developed from any one species, the nearest allies of that species, _i.e._ the species of the same genus, will be the most liable to extermination.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On Extinction”. Scope: species within genera and families

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Turnover among close relatives can be analyzed, but the decisive causal variables are rarely present. Existing data resolve proxies and selected systems, not the general mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct ancestor-descendant or close-relative sets and compare extinction risk following descendant origination as a function of ecological and phylogenetic similarity. Support requires elevated parent and congener extinction beyond environmental and background-rate controls.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Shared environmental responses mimic competitive replacement.

Direct parent-descendant relationships are rarely identifiable.

Superiority is not directly observed.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.43
operationalizability: 0.67
discriminating power: 0.34
analysis feasibility: 0.51
data existence: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The pattern of which relatives disappear first is measurable only where a phylogeny and a fossil record coincide, a small part of the stated scope. Causation by competition is a further inference that co-extinction under a shared environment also predicts. A small team could run the test for planktonic foraminifera or mammals and would not cover genera in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In clades that have both a species-level phylogeny and fossil occurrences, test whether the closest relatives disappear sooner after a species originates than more distant members of the family. Preferential loss of the parent and congeners, beyond shared habitat, would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Species-level trees tied to occurrences cover only a few groups.

Parent and descendant are rarely separable from sister species in the fossil record.

Close relatives share climates and habitats, so they can disappear together without competition between them.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.4
analysis feasibility: 0.45
data existence: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.4
operationalizability: 0.55
